transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Um, yeah—thanks. I guess what finally scared me into coming in is work stuff. I’m a camera operator and editor, and I keep making these really dumb technical mistakes that I absolutely know better than to make.

Like, I’ll label camera cards wrong, or miss a timecode note, or I’ll export a client cut and somehow the wrong lower-third is still in there—even after I checked it. And that’s the part that freaks me out, because I’m not new at this. I have systems, or I try to, anyway. I mean, in production everyone’s always juggling a million tiny details, and some of the software updates don’t help—sorry, that’s beside the point.

It’s just… I keep catching myself making mistakes that could really mess things up professionally, and it’s starting to feel like I can’t trust my own eyes.
Have problems with attention to detail and making careless mistakes been present since childhood?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, the way I remember it, even in elementary school it was kind of a thing—teachers would move my desk around because I was always popping out of my seat or blurting out answers before I was called on.

And I’d be bothering the kids next to me, not even on purpose exactly—like I’d realize after the teacher got mad that I’d been talking or poking at someone’s pencil case or whatever. Sorry, I know you asked about careless mistakes specifically, but… yeah, the school stuff was there early.
Do you often have trouble sustaining your attention on tasks, even when you’re trying to focus?

I’m… not totally sure how to answer that. I mean, I can focus sometimes, especially if something is urgent or there’s a deadline and everyone is waiting on it.

But “sustaining attention” sounds kind of broad. Like, are you asking if I drift off mentally, or if I stop and switch tasks? Because in editing, sometimes switching is part of the job—like you’re looking at audio, then color, then notes, and then suddenly you remember the producer wanted that one shot from the second camera angle—sorry, that’s probably not what you mean.

I guess I notice mistakes more than I notice the attention part itself. I’m trying to focus, but I don’t always know where it breaks down.
Do you get easily distracted by things going on around you when you’re trying to work?

I don’t know if it’s “easily distracted” exactly. I mean, on set there are always people moving around and monitors and someone asking for a cable or yelling about lunch being moved, so it’s hard to tell what’s normal distraction versus me.

At home editing, sometimes I’ll notice I’ve lost the thread, but then I start thinking maybe it’s because the room is too quiet, so I put on music, and then the music is wrong, and—sorry, that’s not really answering.

I guess I’m not sure I’ve noticed it clearly as “things around me” pulling me off task. It’s more like I realize afterward that I wasn’t where I thought I was mentally.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about many different things, even when there isn’t an immediate problem?

I’m not sure. I mean, I worry about normal stuff, I guess—work schedules, whether something is going to get delivered on time, if I forgot to reply to somebody—but that also feels kind of built into production work, you know?

When you say “many different things,” do you mean like I’m sitting there worrying for no reason? Because I don’t know that I notice it that way. I’m usually reacting to whatever’s in front of me, or what I think I’m supposed to be doing next. So… I don’t think I can clearly say yes to that.
Do you often have trouble organizing tasks or keeping track of the steps you need to do things?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, my work already has a lot of moving parts—shot lists, timelines, notes, files, versions—and sometimes it looks disorganized from the outside, but it makes sense to me in the moment.

Keeping track of steps… maybe? I usually just start doing the thing and then figure out the next piece as I go, but I don’t know if that’s trouble organizing or just the way editing works. Like, you fix one cut, then you notice the sound, then you remember the color pass, and then—actually, that’s not really what you asked.

I guess I haven’t really thought of it as a clear problem with organizing tasks. I’d probably need an example of what you mean.
Do you often have trouble following through on tasks and end up leaving things unfinished?

I don’t know that I can say “often,” honestly. I mean, there are things that sit around half-done, but sometimes that’s because the project changes or someone gives notes and then it becomes a totally different thing. In editing, nothing is ever really finished until somebody takes it away from you, which is maybe not what you mean.

Like at home, I’ll start something and then realize I need to move a file, and then I remember the hard drive with the cable that only works if it’s angled right—sorry, that’s probably beside the point.

I guess I’ve noticed unfinished things sometimes, but I’m not sure if it’s a pattern of me not following through or just normal work chaos. I’d need to think about it more.
Do you often feel unable to stop or control your worrying?

I don’t really know. “Unable to control” sounds kind of… bigger than what I notice.

If I’m worried about something specific, like whether a cut is going to be ready or if someone’s waiting on me, I can get stuck checking or thinking about it for a bit. But I don’t know if that’s worrying exactly, or just trying not to drop the ball. And then usually something else comes in—an email, a note, somebody asking for a file—and I’m onto that.

So I guess I wouldn’t clearly say I feel unable to stop worrying. I’m not sure I track it that way.
Do you often lose things you need for work or daily life, like keys, drives, cables, or paperwork?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I misplace stuff sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s more than anyone else.

With work gear it gets confusing because there are just… so many small things. Drives, adapters, card readers, that one cable that only works with that one setup. Sometimes I’ll think something is gone and then it’s in a different pouch or still plugged into a machine from the night before. But I wouldn’t immediately say I “often lose” things.

Keys and paperwork… I don’t know. Paperwork is barely paperwork anymore, it’s all PDFs and links and folders named badly by whoever sent them—sorry, that’s not really the question. I guess I haven’t noticed a clear pattern.
Do you spend a lot of your day feeling tense or on edge, even when nothing urgent is happening?

I’m not totally sure. I don’t think of myself as tense all day when nothing’s happening, but I guess “nothing urgent” is kind of rare in my head because there’s always some file, or a message, or something I should be checking.

But tense like physically on edge? I don’t know. Sometimes I realize my shoulders are up, but that could be from sitting at the computer too long, or bad chairs—editing bays always have the worst chairs, and people act like one fancy monitor fixes everything.

Sorry, I’m wandering. I guess I haven’t really noticed whether it’s a lot of the day or not. I’d have to pay attention to it more.
Do you often put off tasks because they take a lot of sustained mental effort?

I’m not sure. I mean, I do put things off sometimes, but I don’t know if it’s specifically because they take sustained mental effort.

Some tasks just feel like they need the right setup, like I need all the materials open, the notes, the timeline, the version history—sorry, I’m thinking of work stuff. And then sometimes just getting started takes longer than the actual task, which is annoying.

But I don’t know if I’d say I often avoid them for that reason. I guess I haven’t really separated that out in my head.
Outside of work, do these attention problems also cause trouble in everyday life?

I’m not totally sure. I mean, outside work is where things are supposed to be simpler, right? But then everyday life has all these tiny moving parts too—appointments, groceries, remembering which app has which bill, or whether I replied to someone’s message, and then there’s always some random household thing that becomes a whole project.

But I don’t know if I’d clearly call it “attention problems causing trouble.” Sometimes life just feels badly organized in general, if that makes sense. Like every system wants you to have a login and a code and a backup email, and I start thinking, who designed this?

Sorry—outside work, I guess I haven’t really tracked it enough to say for sure. I notice little hassles, but I’m not sure if it’s a real pattern or just normal life stuff.
Do you often interrupt people or answer before they’ve finished speaking?

Yeah… I think I do that. Especially at work. Like if a director or a client starts asking something, I’ll jump in with the answer before they’ve actually finished the question.

And then sometimes halfway through me answering, I realize, oh—wait, that’s not what they were asking. I reacted to the first few words and kind of ran with it. Which is embarrassing, because then I have to back up and be like, “Sorry, what did you mean?” or pretend I was just adding context, which probably fools no one.

It’s not that I’m trying to be rude. I just get ahead of the sentence, I guess.
At home, do you often forget everyday tasks like paying bills, keeping appointments, or returning messages?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, bills are mostly on autopay now, because at some point every company made its own portal and password rules, and I got tired of trying to remember which one was which. So that kind of hides whether I’d forget them or not.

Appointments… I use my phone calendar, but then if it’s not in there, it basically doesn’t exist. Returning messages is harder to judge, because sometimes I see something and think, “I’ll answer when I can say it properly,” and then the day turns into, like, three other things.

But I don’t know if I’d say I often forget everyday tasks exactly. Some things slip around, but I haven’t really kept track of it that way.
Have these problems caused clear difficulties in more than one part of your life, such as both work and home?

I guess the clearest place is work. At home it’s harder for me to say cleanly, because there are all these little things and I don’t know what counts as “clear difficulty.”

But at work, yes. My producers have definitely started trusting me less on more complicated shoots. Like, if it’s a straightforward camera day, my actual camera work is good, and people say that, which is part of why this is so frustrating. But when there are a lot of moving pieces, I can tell they hesitate to put me in charge of that.

And I’ve been hoping to move toward a senior director of photography role, but that feels like it’s slipping away. Not because the image quality isn’t there—it is—but because they don’t seem as confident in me handling the complexity around it. So… yeah, that part has caused real difficulty.
Have these same problems ever caused trouble in your relationships?

Yeah, I think so. Not like… huge blowups all the time, but it does come up.

I catch myself cutting into conversations, especially if I think I know where someone is going with something. And with assistants or people I’m working with closely, I’ve done this thing where I’ll sort of lean over their shoulder and start fixing something on their timeline before they’ve actually asked me to. In my head I’m like, “Oh, I can help, this will be faster,” but I know it can come off like I don’t trust them.

And then afterward I’m thinking, why did I do that? Because I do trust them, or I want to. It just kind of… jumps out of me before I’ve thought through how it lands.
Do you often feel restless, like you need to keep moving or can’t sit still?

Yeah. Especially in client screenings, actually. I can sit there and I know I’m supposed to just be quiet and watch the cut, because that’s the whole point, but it starts feeling like there’s this pressure building under my skin.

Like I need to stand up, or adjust something, or go do literally anything with my body. And it’s weird because I’m not always bored exactly—sometimes I care a lot about what we’re watching—but staying still through it feels… physically uncomfortable. Like my body is waiting for permission to move.

Yeah, I think so. Not like… huge blowups all the time, but it does come up.

I catch myself cutting into conversations, especially if I think I know where someone is going with something. And with assistants or people I’m working with closely, I’ve done this thing where I’ll sort of lean over their shoulder and start fixing something on their timeline before they’ve actually asked me to. In my head I’m like, “Oh, I can help, this will be faster,” but I know it can come off like I don’t trust them.

And then afterward I’m thinking, why did I do that? Because I do trust them, or I want to. It just kind of… jumps out of me before I’ve thought through how it lands.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has a core adult ADHD symptom of restlessness/hyperactivity, which would help distinguish ADHD from anxiety disorders given the unclear anxiety history.
doctor.question: Do you often feel restless, like you need to keep moving or can’t sit still?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: Sitting still through a client screening feels like there’s pressure building under my skin, like I need to get up and do something with my body even when I know I’m supposed to just watch quietly.
target_item.reason: The question directly asks about feeling restless and needing to keep moving or being unable to sit still.

patient.answer:
Yeah. Especially in client screenings, actually. I can sit there and I know I’m supposed to just be quiet and watch the cut, because that’s the whole point, but it starts feeling like there’s this pressure building under my skin.

Like I need to stand up, or adjust something, or go do literally anything with my body. And it’s weird because I’m not always bored exactly—sometimes I care a lot about what we’re watching—but staying still through it feels… physically uncomfortable. Like my body is waiting for permission to move.

inference.note: Restlessness/feeling unable to sit still, impulsive interrupting, childhood onset with hyperactive behaviors, and impairment at work and in relationships support ADHD and make primary anxiety disorders less likely.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a persistent pattern since childhood of hyperactive/impulsive behavior and current inattentive-type errors causing occupational and interpersonal impairment. Confirmed symptoms include childhood leaving seat and blurting out answers, current interrupting/answering before others finish, restlessness/inability to stay still, and recurrent careless mistakes at work. Symptoms are longstanding, began in childhood, and now impair work performance and relationships. Anxiety symptoms were queried but not clearly endorsed, making ADHD the best fit.
